title: The switch Statement
description: Choosing one of many fixed values, the break you must not forget, and the modern arrow form.

content.text: Press 3 and the lift goes straight to floor 3. A `switch` takes one value and jumps straight to the matching case, instead of asking `day == 1`, `day == 2`... one by one.

content.title: Fall-through
content.outro: This is called **fall-through**: running on into the next case. It compiles fine, so the output is your only clue.

content.question: No `break` anywhere, `day = 2`. What prints?
content.explain: Java jumps to `case 2`, then falls through every case below it, including `default`.

content.caption: Fall-through on purpose: stacked cases with no code between them share one block. Days 6 and 7 both reach `Weekend!`.

items: A switch works on an `int`, a `char` or a `String`.
With a `String` it matches by content, so no `.equals` is needed.
Text matching is case sensitive: `"yes"` and `"Yes"` are different cases.

content.value: A case must be a fixed value. `case age > 18:` is not allowed. For ranges and comparisons, use an `else if` chain.

content.caption: Write `->` instead of `:`. Each case runs only its own line: no fall-through, so no `break` to forget. Group values with commas.

parts.label: cases
parts.note: Each `case 3 -> "Wednesday";` inside gives the value for one match.

content.title: A switch that gives a value
content.caption: The arrow form can produce a value. Note the `;` after the closing `}`: it is all one statement.
One variable, one assignment, every day accounted for. A block in braces also works when a case needs several lines.

content.value: Both tools pick one path out of many. The deciding question is: fixed values, or ranges?

items.title: switch
items.text: One value against a list of **fixed** values: menu options, day numbers, grade letters.

content.title: switch or else if?
content.caption: You will read both switch forms in real code. When writing new code, prefer the arrow form: less to go wrong.

content.question: Which tool fits "temperature above 30 is hot, above 20 is warm"?
content.explain: These are ranges. A switch can only match fixed values, so use an `else if` chain.

quiz.question: What does `break` do inside a switch?
options: Ends the switch, so Java does not run the cases below
quiz.explain: Without it, Java falls through into the next case and keeps going until it finds a `break` or reaches the end.

quiz.question: A switch on `day` matches `case 1`, which has no `break`. What happens?
options: The cases below it also run, until a break is found
The program stops with an error
quiz.explain: This is fall-through. It compiles cleanly, so the wrong output is the only sign that a `break` is missing.

quiz.question: What is `default` in a switch?
options: The catch-all, like the final `else` in a chain
The case that always runs first
A required label on every case
quiz.explain: `default` runs when no case matched. Leaving it out means an unexpected value does nothing at all.

quiz.question: Which of these can a switch NOT do?
quiz.explain: A switch compares against fixed known values only. Ranges and comparisons need an `else if` chain.

quiz.question: Why does the arrow form `case 6, 7 -> ...` need no `break`?
options: Each arrow case runs only its own code: there is no fall-through.
It has an invisible break added by the compiler at run time.
It does need one, but only for the last case.
quiz.explain: The arrow form was designed to remove the trap. Values that share a block are listed with commas instead of by stacking labels.

quiz.question: When switching on a `String`, do you need `.equals`?
options: No: a switch compares text by content already.
Yes, but only in the default case.
quiz.explain: The switch handles the comparison correctly for you. It is still case sensitive, so `"Yes"` and `"yes"` are separate cases.
